utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Always a better feeling on Friday. Certainly much better than it is on Monday. So I wish you all good morning in anticipation of a good weekend. Madam Registrar, if you could kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, madam. So all the accused are here. I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Haynes. I can't see behind. Yes, Mr. Haynes. And on the part of the Prosecution now, we have Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. The witness is here. Good morning to you, Mr. Medic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I'm happy to greet you again. Hopefully we will finish with your testimony today so that you can go back to your family. Yesterday morning, Mr. Nikolic had started with the preliminaries. Today we will go into more substance. You've got all the time you requested, Mr. Nikolic, to proceed with and finish your examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you and everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before we go into the substance I just wanted to remind ourselves where we left it off yesterday so as to make it easier. Mr. Medic, your last answer yesterday had to do with the organisation of the military courts and the fact that the military court of Split was relocated to Tivat. Split is in Croatia, and Tivat is in Montenegro. In 1992 you were in the investigative judge of the military court in Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was an investigative judge working for the military court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That same year you conducted an investigation against Ljubisa Beara and a group of soldiers as well as another officer for the crime of instigation murder; is that correct, instigating to commit a murder?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was the military court in Belgrade competent to carry out and investigation in that case?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't geographically competent to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How did it come about, then, and how was it that it was possible for the military court to conduct that investigation and to entrust you with that investigation in particular?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a possibility for that in the law. If I may, I can explain to you how that came about. It was in early July 1992. I was summoned by the president of the court who told me that in Debeli Brijeg, in Montenegro, on a border crossing to Croatia there was a double murder of the soldiers or members of the Territorial Defence - I don't know what they were exactly - and that the top echelon of the army decided that that investigation should be carried out by the military court in Belgrade. He appointed me as the judge in charge of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I suppose that it was preceded by certain legal documentation because, indeed, the law envisages that the jurisdiction of one court can be delegated to another. Did you have occasion to see those documents? Were they presented to you before you took over the investigation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you with any degree of certainty now. I don't remember whether I saw the decision of the supreme military court on the delegation of territorial jurisdiction to the court in Belgrade. However, without that document it would have been difficult to do anything. I suppose that the decision existed; however, I cannot tell you with any certainty whether I saw it and if at all and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. So you took over the case file, and you took measures in order to launch an investigation against these persons. What was your first task, the first action that you undertook within that investigation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can first tell you about the whole course of my preparations to go to Montenegro if that would be of any interest to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is exactly what I meant. What happened from the moment when you were tasked with the case onwards?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure as I sit here, because it was 16 years ago, whether the President of the Court told me that there was a vehicle waiting for me, or maybe the chief of the security administration of the army, General Boskovic, called me and told me that a car would pick me up. I really don't know who told me that, but soon after that, maybe half an hour or an hour later, a vehicle did come. In the meantime, I called the forensic pathologist from the VMA, and I believe that a military Prosecutor went together with us, if I remember it well. I believe it was the late Tomislav Cvetkovic, but I'm not sure. In General Boskovic's vehicle, we were taken to the General Staff to General Boskovic's office, and that is where General Boskovic showed me a report by the security service of the command of the navy from Kumbor with a brief description of what had happened, and that was my first encounter with the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the security administration in General Boskovic's office, you received the initial information on where you were supposed to go and what had happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He briefly told me about the incident, maybe in a sentence or two, and he was in a hurry. He gave me the report. I believe that it was a teleprinted report from the navy command in Kumbor. He also told us that a plane was waiting for us and that we were supposed to fly to Tivat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who was it who provided the plane? Was it a regular Belgrade Tivat flight, or was it a special flight; and who provided that flight?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a military plane. I don't know who provided it. In any case, it was the General Staff of the air force. It was a Falcon plane with 12 seats. It was a passenger aircraft but it belonged to the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, you were an investigating judge for a number of years. Did you often have such conditions in place when you had to carry out investigations. Was that something that happened very often?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an exceptional situation. I believe it happened only once or twice. In other cases, we had to make due as we could using public transportation, trains, cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So why was this an exceptional situation in your view? Were there any legal foundations for this to be so exceptionally well organised, since you said yourself that in your everyday life and in all the other cases you had to make do and you had to find your own means?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view it was not an exceptional case. It was a case like any other. Why it was organised in that way by the General Staff, I really can't tell you. I can't account for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well then. You take off -- you took off at Tivat. Who was on the plane with you?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Nedjo Boskovic; Dr. Zoran Stankovic, the forensic pathologist; and I believe the deputy prosecutor Tomislav Svetkovic was also with us, but I'm not sure about the last name, although I believe that he was with us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Why would General Boskovic who was the chief of the security administration travel with investigating judge? Did he maybe have something else to attend to in Tivat?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer that. I suppose that he had some other things to attend to. What his interest in the whole matter was, I don't know, save for the fact that these people were his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During your flight to Tivat, did you discuss the case? Did you talk to General Boskovic and to the other passengers on the flight at all?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the plane I spoke to General Boskovic, and he told me about the case that Dr. Vojislav Seselj, the president of the Serbian radical party - I believe that it was its name at the time - had called the general -- the chief of the General Staff, General Panic. He was very angry, and he called for a very detailed investigation. That's what he told me about the case. I don't know whether he told me anything else, but this I know for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about that on the plane, what conclusions did you arrive at after this conversation? Did you arrive at any conclusions?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could sense pressure, and I could feel that there was pressure being put on me, but I did not let the pressure get to me. The way things had been organised, the way the plane had been organised, it's all pointed to the fact that this was an important matter. But it did not have any bearing on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When given such an explanation by General Boskovic, did you deem it important to warn him that you would not succumb to any pressures, and did you explain yourself to him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I've been letting it go, but there's been some leading of the witness. I'm now objecting to further leading, and the bigger picture, I'm not sure yet what the probative value so far is and if it can be reached sooner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, but you knew exactly what this witness was going to testify about, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This might sound like something strange in legal terms. Given the subject matter that we are dealing with, or rather, that the witness is dealing with and the great detail in which Mr. Nikolic is leading the witness to, we believe that the best way to cut it short is as follows: First, to encourage Mr. Nikolic to sift the grain from the chaff and concentrate on what is important for your client when it comes to this witness and go straight to the point. I mean, we don't need fine details that will get you and us nowhere and will involve some more expense of time. The second thing that is given the subject matter, we believe that allowing Mr. Nikolic to lead is perhaps the speediest way of bringing the testimony of this gentleman to a quick end. I don't know whether you would be prepared to live with that, and the same applies to Mr. Nikolic. I think Mr. Nikolic would definitely be in favour of what I have stated, but perhaps the Prosecution on second thoughts would agree as well. There is a reason why we were allowing leading questions too. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'll withdraw my objection for the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are trying to be as practical and pragmatic as possible and hoping that Mr. Nikolic will be too. Thank you. Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I was just going to go to the heart of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, what was the first thing that you did when you arrived in Tivat and embarked on your investigation?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a very short answer to that. When I arrived in Tivat, I learned that my colleague from the Tivat military court Judge Radomir Besevic [phoen] had already carried out an onsite inspection, and I really wasn't clear why I should do all that again. I felt uncomfortable. I had to apologise to him. He even showed me the record of the onsite inspection, and here I was, having to do all that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you interview the accused Beara?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Having carried out an onsite inspection, I interviewed the suspects, Mr. Ljubisa Beara and two or three others whose names I can't remember. One of them I believe was Pag and a junior officer, but I can't remember their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How did Mr. Beara behave? Did he respond to your summons as the investigating judge, and did he come for the interview?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. Beara came without any problem. Not only him but everybody else turned up for the interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt. No objection. It just might save time on cross. I wonder if I could get the -- I think its clear but the time frame of when this interviewing is occurring. If it's directly after the killings or if it's at some point later. It wasn't completely clear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would take it for granted, but yes. Please, Mr. Nikolic, if you could put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, when you interviewed Mr. Beara, the accused in this case, did Mr. Beara pose any obstructions? Did he object to the investigation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know whether it could be a question of interpretation, but my suggestion to you, Mr. Nikolic, was that you ask the witness to state the time frame when he interviewed Mr. Beara. That is, whether it was immediately after the killings or whether there had been a lapse of time, in which case we would like to know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, obviously there was a misunderstanding due to the interpretation. I did not understand your question at first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, how much time lapsed from your first conversation with your colleague to the moment when you summoned Mr. Beara and interviewed him, and how much time elapsed between that and your arrival in Tivat?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the Prosecutor's question as wanting to know how much time lapsed between the incident and the interview. In any case, there were three or four days from the event to my arrival, and I carried out the onsite inspection on the same day when I arrived, and I believe that on the same day or on the following day I interviewed Mr. Beara and the other suspects. I can't answer this question with any degree of reliability. I know that the interviews took place in the evening, but I don't know whether it was on the same day when I arrived or the day after my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you interviewed Mr. Beara, did you remand him in custody, and could you please just briefly give us the legal foundation for any such decision.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having interviewed Mr. Beara and other suspects, I believe that there were two. I ordered them to be remanded in custody, and I told each and every one of them that Mr. Beara behaved as a true gentleman. He did not object. He behaved in a very proper manner, and if you wanted to hear the legal foundations for the custody, first of all you have to bear in mind the gravity of the crime that had been committed over there. The legal foundations would be influencing witnesses, disturbance for the general public, and a very strange climate had been created, and I wanted, amongst other things, to isolate Mr. Beara from the area, and custody was one way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you say that the climate was strange, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could feel tensions among all the members of the navy whom I contacted. Even the general population was highly strung, and the latter was one of the main reasons why I ordered the suspects to be remanded in custody. In addition to that, I came by information that Mr. Beara had come under certain threats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Who did the threats come from? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but I believe that the threats came from the circles close to the victims of the murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The victims were members of the Territorial Defence as you've told us. Which region did they hail from?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they were members of the Territorial Defence in Herzegovina either in Bilici or in Trebinje; I'm not sure, and I believe that they were volunteers of the Serb radical party.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Medic, you carried out the investigation. We know that was completed, and then the case was forwarded to the Prosecutor for further processing.

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the results or the outcome of the proceedings or procedure was? I know that you were not the judge in charge of the trial itself, but it took place at your court in Belgrade, so what was the final outcome of the case?

utterances.speaker: VOJISLAV MEDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer with any certainty. There were several trials. There were several judgements and then appeals, and it seemed to go around about two or three times. I don't know what the final decision was, but according to some information Mr. Beara did not receive a prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Medic. For your information, Mr. Beara was acquitted concerning the charge of instigating murder, and for the other charge he received a probationary sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my examination. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Now, let's do the round. Mr. Zivanovic, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll not cross-examine this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic, you had asked for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions for the witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gosnell, you had asked for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau, you had asked, also, for ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci, madam. We don't know, but I would assume you are not much interested in this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you. And Mr. Sarapa? Equally so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No. Yes, no questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, you had asked for an hour and a half. If you need two hours, we are prepared to extend it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, I hope you won't hold it against me, Your Honours, but we weren't sure exactly what the witness was going to say. I have no questions at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Medic, I don't know if you've broken the record on this trial, but your testimony is over in a few minutes. Roughly we've taken just over half an hour between yesterday and today. You are free to go back to your family and work. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, my colleagues, and the supporting staff, I would like to thank you very much for being so kind to come over and telling us all about these events, and on behalf of everyone present I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish you all very fruitful work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it we have no documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. No documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That concludes the testimony of Vojislav Medic. Next witness. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Morning, Mr. President. The next witness is our 2DW-11, which is Ljubomir Mitrovic, who was at one point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure it's the same one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, let's wait for madam usher to bring him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not even sure if he is here this morning. I haven't seen him, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't be surprised if he isn't because we finished a little bit earlier than expected. On the other hand, again, without chastising the newcomer, Mr. Nikolic, and directing myself to you or rather Mr. Ostojic, given the substance of the evidence of this witness, I wonder how it circulated around the corridors of your mind, of your brains, to indicate that you required two hours for this witness's testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when we proofed the witness it actually took a lot longer, and we just wanted to make sure that we were not barred from going over the initial estimate, which was made several months ago without actually ever meeting the witness. I mean, I met him the first time this past few days, so we just wanted to be safe, and we felt with respect to the next witness, since the Prosecution estimated an hour and a half and we weren't informed at all that they would have anything less than that, and given the exhibits that they produced potentially to be used with the exhibit -- with this witness, we felt rather safe that it was going to take us to at least the very first break. And I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ostojic. Madam, we are investigating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please -- all right, that's perfectly understandable. I mean, when these things happen, we'll have to learn to adjust accordingly. We are informed that the next witness was scheduled to be brought over towards 12.30. That's taking into account, of course, the two hours that were required by you, the hour and a half that were required by the Prosecution, more or less; that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were trying to discuss how we could all together pull a little bit more effort and try to be more efficient in this. But I'm pretty sure that you will try. Independently of this, we are informed that this gentleman was scheduled to come over at 12.30. Our staff is trying to locate him, make sure that -- if he is still in his hotel, in which case they will bring him over in a matter of between 20 and 30 minutes, and we can resume the sitting. If he is not in the hotel, we may have problems, but I would all ask you to stand by, have a coffee or whatever, but stay inside the building because we could resume any time and at the first opportunity he is found and brought over. All right? Thank you. --- Break taken at 9.44 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you do so, I wish to tell you that you are required to make a solemn declaration, equivalent to an oath in certain jurisdictions, that the course of your testimony you will be testifying the truth. Madam usher is going to hand you now the text of this solemn declaration. Once you've made it, that will be your solemn commitment with us. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. You've been summoned as a witness by the Defence team for Colonel Beara here, so it will be that Defence team that will go first with some questions. They will be followed by others on cross-examination. Is it Mr. Ostojic? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, as you know my name is John Ostojic, and I represent -- we represent Mr. Beara here in this case. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you just -- so we have it in the record, can you tell us your full name?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Ljubomir Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us your date of the birth and where you presently reside?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The 27th of September, 1939. I currently reside in Bijeljina in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise for asking you this question, sir, but sometime it is seems relevant in these proceedings. Can you tell us what your ethnic affiliation is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, forgive me fore asking your religious affiliation, if any?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'm an atheist.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you could give us a little more background about yourself so we could have a better understand of what you did during your life and specifically in 1995. Tell us a little bit about your educational background. What is the greatest level of education that you completed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I completed the teachers academy, which is at the level of high school, and then two years of academy specializing in chemistry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And can you just tell us where you worked approximately in the late 1980s to early 1990s, if at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: During that time, I worked for the state security until 1985. And that year, I transferred to the public security sector. In 1986, I was appointed commander of the municipal staff of TO for Bijeljina under the proviso that after four years I was to return again to the ministry of the interior. In 1991, my mandate ran out; however, I did not return to the ministry because I was not a member of the parties that won at the time. That party in particular was the Serb democratic party. As I was expected to join the party when assuming my previous position, I did not do so, and I requested that I be retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just help me again, what year was that that -- 1991 that you requested that you -- to retire?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What, if anything, did you do from 1991 through let's just say September or December of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In 1991 when I retired, I took some time to rest and to get away from all the problems that have plagued all of our nations. In December 1991, I was summoned to the command of the 38th Partisan Brigade. That command was being in formation, and they told me that they were short of staff since they could no longer count on any Muslim or Croat colleagues. Knowing that I had worked for the security services, I was offered to be the head of the security organ of the 38th Brigade. I knew the commander from before; therefore, I wasn't ordered to do so, although in military terms, that should have been so. I requested some time to take my time before assuming position, but it didn't take place. I remained at the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain at that unit, the 38th Partisan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there until late May 1992. On the 20th of May, the active duty professional officers were supposed to go to Serbia and Montenegro if they wanted to, and the few officers there were left. The command was disbanded, and I was transferred to the 17th partisan brigade in charge of the security organ. In a few months time, it was to be renamed to the 1st Semberija brigade the same year my brigade went to Majevica, which is a mountain; and I was there until mid-March 1993, after which I was transferred to the corps, to the security department there. I was also appointed a member of the commission for the exchange of POWs and the mortal remains of those killed. I was a member of the commission, and I worked in my capacity according to the rules. I wasn't a decision-maker with the commission, and on several occasions I visited Batkovic, and I also had frequent contacts with other members of the commission as well as the other party's commission and representatives of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. We are going to break that down a little bit if you don't mind, sir, and specifically what I'd like to know is, you were initially from your testimony a member of the commissioner for exchange of prisoners and bodies. That commission was of the East Bosnia Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A little more background, sir, before we ask what your job duties and responsibilities were in connection with that. How long were you a member of this commission as a member of the commission, meaning not as we know you became president subsequently, so I want to just break it down. Were you a member for a short period of time, or did you become president of this commission immediately thereafter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As of mid-March 1993 until the 20th of April, 1994, I was a member of the commission. It was then that I was made president by the corps commander's order. I was appointed president of the exchange commission. That lasted until the 30th of April, 1997. After that, the commission no longer existed; I was demobilized and went home. I requested that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mitrovic. Let me focus if I can with you the period when you were a member of this Commission for Exchange of Prisoners and Bodies. How many people were in this commission with you, again, during the period you were there, 1993 through 20th of April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In total there were five members on the commission: The president, and that was an establishment post; then there was a secretary. That was another establishment post. As for the rest, they came from various units. They had their primary duties with those units but, also, when the commission met they were supposed to join the commission and work with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, can you share with me who at that time was the president of the commission, from 1993 through the time April 20th, 1994, when you became president, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was Matija Bodirogic from Tuzla. He was a refugee in Bijeljina. Do you need me to tell you anything about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We may, but it you could just be kind enough to share with us if you recall some of the other members of the commission during that time period, 1993 through 1994.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The secretary, Mitra Radovanovic. There were changes taking place. There was Sokic, I think he was a warrant officer; and Makso Simeonovic from Brcko. He was to remain with the commission for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, during that period of 1993 through 1994 when you were a member of this commission, can you describe for me what the commission was doing as a whole? What were your job duties and responsibilities at that time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The commission established contacts with the commissions from the Federation and occasionally from Croatia, as well, depending on the need. It was done by the commission member from Brcko because he had radio communication. Occasionally, we made use of other types of communication from Bijeljina. There were quite a number of bodies on both sides to be exchanged as of early 1992 when the fighting began. First, we would negotiate in order to ascertain whether there were any bodies, and then we wanted to know how many and what the opposing party wanted in return. Those problems could not be dealt with in one blow. There were some problems as far back as 1991, and once the commission was disbanded there were still problems expected to be resolved. We also had contacts with the ICRC. They were looking for some people, and we wanted to gain some information from them. We had good cooperation, and things went as they should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just so I can clarify, you said that you established contacts with the Federation and contacts with Croatia. When you say the Federation, you had -- did you have a counterpart on the Bosnian Muslim side that you would enter into these negotiations or discussions with, sir, in 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As for the Federation commission, from the moment I joined our commission until the end there was always somebody that I had known, either we had worked together; some people I knew from the Territorial Defence regional staff; some people were from the state security service. There was also a committee secretary from Bijeljina from the time when I had been a member of the committee. There was always someone I knew on the other side, and I believe that contributed to an exceptionally good cooperation we had, and that was the opinion shared by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just tell me the name of the commission in 1993/1994 from the Federation that you had contacts and dealings with with respect to the exchange of prisoners and bodies.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, it was the commission of the Tuzla canton. There may have been one meeting with the Zenica Canton Commission, but that's where we ran into most of the problems. There were the most difficult problems to be resolved with them. The Tuzla Canton Commission comprised some 15 municipalities. There were far more numerous in terms of members of the commission, whereas on our side there were always four or five. They, however, had one representative per each town or municipality. There was also some discussion concerning civilians, and at the beginning there were some exchanges - I don't know how many, exactly - that involved the civilian population, of course, following the approvals of both sides' authorities. There were some exchanges, and certain people were sought after who had been in prison. However, we established that they were no longer in prisons, and we continued with that type of civilian exchanges. At a later point, we gave up from exchanging civilians, and we continued exchanging soldiers only.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We'll get into that in a little more detail when you became president of this commission, but again, just if we can focus for the time being on the '93 and '94 so I can get a better understanding, and we all can, as to what -- thank you, as to what was going on. Now, you mentioned that you were a member of this commission of the -- it's in the title. It says the East Bosnian Corps. Can you tell us were there other similarly situated commissions in the other corps areas of the former territory of Bosnia, meaning the 1st Krajina, the 2nd Krajina, the Herzegovina Krajina, the Sarajevo-Romanija corps, and the Drina Corps. Did you have similar type commissions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: All of the corps had their own exchange commissions, all of them at the time. They had exchange commissions for the exchange of POWs. It would have been impossible to have one corps commission working in such a large area and dealing with such extensive problems. If we are talking about meetings, then occasionally we would have two commissions on our side meeting with the commissions of the other side at the state level. We will have the state commission of the Serb side meeting the state commission of the Federation, and that will usually take place in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And with respect to your answer that all the corps had their own exchange commission, do you know when they were formed in each of the corps if they were not formed at the same time? Do you know approximately when they were formed, these commissions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know when they were officially established, but something was in existence already. Perhaps it wasn't called commission, but each of the corps had something. Once combat began, there was an immediate need to exchange bodies of those killed. It was, therefore, sometime in 1992, but I don't know when exactly and in what official capacity or by what name, but in any case exchanges were underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, help us with this: Do you know or do you recall whether or not in 1993 the commissions existed into each of the corps that we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to see that myself and to meet some of the presidents of those commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you discussed briefly the need or the immediate need to exchange bodies of those killed. Were there exchanges of soldiers in that period when you were just a member of the commission from 1993 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: We didn't have any, but those corps which had soldiers captured did exchange them. We did have people who had been killed from the Posavina theatre, and that's when -- where they were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did the commission from the East Bosnia Corps which you became the president ultimately form, if at all, a detention centre or camp?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The commission did not establish a collection centre or a camp. I don't know what it was exactly. It was established in 1992, but I don't know under whose orders. I was at Majevica at the time. I do know it was formed that year and that it was used to have the prisoners from the other corps brought in to a single centre. That's why I use the term "collection centre." I don't know at what time it was, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know the name of that collection centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The collection centre of Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's talk about Batkovici for a few minutes here. Is that the collection centre that you say was established in 1992?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been there, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Not up to the time when I transferred to the commission for exchange. Basically I never went there. I only went home every fortnight or so to take a shower, but prior to my arrival to the corps, I had no knowledge of the existence of that centre. Once with the corps to become a member of the commission -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, no, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the corps as a member of the commission, I had occasion to meet the people from the command of the collection centre. It was then that I learned where it was and what the status of the detainees was. I was interested in that. One of the reasons why I asked to go to Majevica and to be returned to my brigade was because I put forth a request that if the detainees are to be beaten or maltreated, I would be refuse to be a member of the commission since I would be too ashamed to negotiate. I think that had a bearing, since I was unable to order anything in Batkovic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Baljkovica"] the commander at the time was someone who was with me in the Semberija brigade. We could talk as friends so that I would be able to work on my duties as best I could with the other side. If you need me to go into any more detail, I'm willing to do so. I went there with representatives of the ICRC, as well, and when they wanted to do so, we could go, and perhaps it was once a week depending on the situation. If I was not busy with other tasks, I would go with them, and it would be on those occasions that I could arrange for something as well. I was there in terms of escort when they wanted to talk to prisoners, and there would be sentries. Sometimes we would leave, as well, so that the detainees could share their concerns or objections if they had any. Also, the representatives of the ICRC never conveyed to me something that would have been of particular interest to me in terms of the detainees being maltreated. They never told me they noticed any irregularities in terms of how those people were treated or that their money was taken or anything of the sort. The cantonal commission never mentioned anything of that either. Quite to the contrary. When I talked to a colleague from Doboj, they told me it's good that these people went to Kotorsko because it's a real jail. Why did they have to leave Batkovici? We know that they faired far better in Batkovici than anywhere else. Any jail is bad in and of itself, but we tried to treat them as humanly as possible. I can also say that they ate the same food as the officers of the corps. There was only one mess, and the food was the same for all. It was rich in terms of nutrition but not very varied; we were not happy, either. When there was a surplus of food, we always shared it with the prisoners. I think they were happy in that regards as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, we were going a little -- and I know we are all anxious. We are going a little further ahead, and we are going to cover those areas, sir, hopefully with you today. But really, my question is if we can focus on the Batkovic camp. Where is it located, or where was it located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It shows the name of the village. The village is Batkovic. It is 7 -- 6 kilometres away from Bijeljina, and as you pass through the village, some 4 kilometres further is the camp, so altogether it's about 10 kilometres from Bijeljina. And since you had to go through the village of Batkovic to get to the collection centre, the name given to it was Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I just wanted to make a correction for the record. We've had this problem before. The names sound familiar, and it's being Baljkovica, which is a different location, and it's Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe for us the premises of the detention centre? What did it look like? Was there one structure? Was it a multi-structure centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The premises were of the former agricultural combine of Batkovic. It was actually called the Semberija farm. The buildings that were there were prefabricated buildings. There, you could see all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. Their purpose was to serve as storages. They were not meant to be residential buildings but, rather, storage for cereals, and since Bijeljina is midway from Herzegovina to Krajina, I suppose this was what made people decide that this would be a collection centre. When it comes to conditions, the conditions were not really what they should be, but we tried to provide mats and blankets - the ICRC also helped - in order to create conditions for the detainees to spend sometime there, though to large hangars to large storage facilities, and there were also adjacent buildings which had housed the combine management back in the day. When I came, only one of the buildings was used, but later on another building was also prepared to accommodate the detainees but was never put in use. Maybe we'll come to that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, just give me a chance to ask the question, and I'm sure we'll get there, sir, soon enough. Focusing on the premises of the Batkovic camp, can you tell me who maintained the premises in 1993 and 1994? Who was in charge of running the camp?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The collection centre had its commander and its command, of course. The commander was subordinated to the corps commander, and it -- he reported to him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did your commission have any involvement with running the detention centre at all or maintaining it or providing any of the food to that facility, or were you a separate and distinction entity?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: We were a separate body because the exchange commission was appointed by the commander. We were supposed to cooperate, but we could not influence one another, especially when it came to the provisions. It was the assistant commander for logistics who took care of that for the collection centre and for the other units, and there are also some other junior officers who were in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we could include the period of when you became president of this commission, as well, in my next question. What is the greatest number of POWs, if you recall, that were maintained at this collection centre up to July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The situation changed in 1992 and 1993. People came and went. For example, the Banja Luka corps would bring a certain number, and they would take them away. There were up to 500 people at any one time. When I became the president of the commission, there were only 40 to 50 of them, and they were not all of them prisoners of war in the proper sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's talk about the period of the -- when you were president of this commission. Were there any other detention centres during the time that you were president other than the one that we mentioned called Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know there were no other collection centres. I don't know about Herzegovina. I never spoke to anybody about that, but I know that the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina corps did not have any. Actually, the 1st Krajina Corps I don't know about because I did not have any contact with them. As for the 2nd Krajina corps and the Drina Corps, they did not have of any such collection centres, but I would like to say this: It did happen that not everybody managed to reach Batkovic. Some would be kept because if the corps needed to conduct exchanges and if there was an opportunity, it would not have been economical to take people there and return them. So they would keep them for a while until they got in touch with the other side or until things were negotiated and agreed upon, and as for the rest they would be taken to Batkovic first, and then when there was an occasion to have them exchanged, they would be taken from Batkovic and brought to the place where each of the commissions had agreed upon the exchange to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Earlier today in your testimony, you were beginning to share with us your view that you instructed people that if you are going to undergo and conduct certain negotiations that you specifically require that the POWs be treated properly, and I just don't -- and I want to ask you this, and we'll talk about that specifically more: When did this happen, sir, in your capacity as a member of the commission or in your capacity as president of the commission? If you could give me the date or the year approximately.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1993, the same year when I joined the commission. I said I could not issue any orders, but I did inform my superior officer on what I was going to say and what I was going to propose to the commander of the collection centre, and this was accepted. The situation was as it was because we were not strictly on official terms. We had been acquaintances and friends for a number of years. When he arrived in January 1993, that's how he behaved. That's one of the reasons, as I've already told you at the very beginning. I told him if any of them were to be beaten in Batkovic, be it Croats or Muslims, the same would happen to the detained Serbs on the other side; and I believe that this was very helpful because people who had been detained from our corps, they were not ill-treated because the news spread very quickly. We did not have to wait until the end of the war to learn what the treatment of the prisoners on both sides was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you maintain this policy or position when you became president of the commission in April of 1994 and through 1997?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: That was my way approach -- that was my way of thinking throughout all my life. You can't expect to do evil by others and fare differently, and as president I probably had a bit more influence than otherwise, but it wasn't even necessary. As far as I can tell you, and I repeat, I did not sleep there; I would only go there occasionally, accompanying the ICRC, and I never learned from the Tuzla commission or the members of the ICRC that there had been any complaints, any mention of ill treatment, at least for as long as I was in the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, covering the period while you were in the position, do you know how often you -- or do you remember how often you would meet with the Tuzla Canton for Exchange Commission in a given month or if it was once a month in a given year, if you could just break it down for us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. There was no plan to meet. We would meet very often. Sometimes it would even happen that we met on one day and then we would have to meet again the following day or within a week even when we did not have prisoners of war in Batkovic that they would be interested in, and when they spoke to the commission of the first -- or actually the 2nd Krajina corps that they would not come to negotiate, I would tell them, I have nothing to offer you; we'll wait until we have prisoners of war and then we can meet. And then the president would say, no, let's meet next week and see what we can do. They even wanted able-bodied men, but I suppose the leadership would not allow them to do that. It was a lot of work because there were about 900 Muslims, able-bodied men, younger men that needed to be looked into. I had to find out where they were. I know that they had all the good intentions, but things were not always simple. We did meet and we tried to talk, and if we did not have prisoners of war to exchange, then we would look at exchanging the bodies of those who had not been exchanged from 1991. In the meantime, we would exchange bodies. We would try to find locations of though who were missing, and so on and so forth. In any case, there were lots of contacts, perhaps even up to seven or eight meetings in a month because it sometimes happened that we could not coordinate ourselves, so we had to consult each other in order to solve the situation. Another commission was established in the municipality of Teocak, which was closer to me, and we spoke even with them, with the consent of the Tuzla commission, and with them we also arranged for the exchange of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, did you also have these meetings with ICRC?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Not official. These meetings were never official, but since my office was in town, maybe four buildings or five buildings away from the ICRC building, we would either talk, or I would drop in when passing the building, or they would come to see me in my office and we would talk. Whenever they could go and assist negotiations, we would inform them and ask them to join us. There was never any problem for them joining us in our negotiations. The ICRC representatives often accompanied the other side, as well, so that was never a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mitrovic, where did these meetings take place, and just if you could be brief a little bit so that I could try to put a couple questions to you. I know you want to share all this, and we will get to it, but just tell us where. Was it always in the Federation side; was it always in Bijeljina, or where when you were president of that commission?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The meetings were always between the lines of the warring parties in that territory, and the places were Satorovici near Brcko; Sibosnica near Lopare; Povrsnica on Mount Majevica near Lopare; the Ban Brdo; the pass on Mount Majevica. We had two meetings. I -- one was a failed attempt, in Memici near Zvornik. That's where the meetings took place most frequently. Later on, we had meetings in Gradacac and Gracanica on one or two occasions. The previous ones were taking place more often.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have any meetings in Sarajevo or near Sarajevo during the July 1995 period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll walk you through that if you don't mind, sir. Sorry to interrupt you. Was that the only time that you had a meeting in Sarajevo, was in July of 1995 with the Tuzla Cantonal Exchange Commission, or did you have other meetings prior to that in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that we had a meeting in January 1995 or maybe in December. There was snow. That's when we had a meeting, and a few days later we had another meeting in Sarajevo, and from there we went to Sidski Brod near Tuzla in the S4 base by United Nations helicopters, and in that military camp we also had a meeting, and that preceded the events in Srebrenica, all these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, sir. Who attended the meeting? Was it just representatives from your commission? Were you the sole representatives, and give us a little more flavour or feeling, if you will, of who was on the other side and whether or not ICRC was present, as well, during those meetings.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: When we had meetings in Sarajevo, those meetings were organised by the state commissions of the Republika Srpska and the Federation; i.e., the presidents of the respective commissions had agreed the principles of the talks, and then we would be invited. Not all the corps were present. Most commonly, it would be the representatives of the Tuzla Canton and the Zenica Canton who would be present and also the Banja Luka or the 1st Krajina Corps as well as the East Bosnia Corps. I am not sure, but I believe that there were representatives of the Drina Corps at one of the meetings, but I'm not sure. And these meetings did not yield any results. Those were mostly negotiations between the presidents of the state commissions on the two sides. The records were taken of what had been done, how commissions had carried out their work. I never wanted to sign any of these minutes or records because they were really not helpful and there was not much use of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and we'll talk about that. Let me ask you this, sir: Do you remember an occasion in July 1995 that you had a meeting in Sarajevo with the Tuzla Cantonal Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: We were supposed to have a meeting in Kiseljak near Sarajevo on the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll talk about that in just a few minutes, but I'd like to understand a little bit more about how the meeting was set up and when it was set up and why it was set up, so if you give me that chance, sir, we'll get to the meeting as soon as possible. You said you were supposed to have a meeting. How much before July 11th, 1995, did you schedule to have a meeting in Kiseljak near Sarajevo with the Tuzla Cantonal Exchange Commission?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was not us who scheduled that. It was the state commissions who scheduled that meeting, and they were the ones who decided who should be present. The corps commissions did not have a say in making a decision whether they would attend or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How much, if you know, before July 11th was this meeting set up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe two days earlier we learned of the meeting, and I don't know when it was scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You were asked to attend this meeting, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And by whom?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The president of the state commission, which, again, went through the corps, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Because the corps command was the command that made any decisions on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We understand that, Mr. Mitrovic. Just help me with this: Do you know prior to going to the meeting on the 11th, 1995, what the purpose of the meeting was going to be?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes. We knew that the Tuzla corps representatives were -- would be there, and that's what we were actually interested in, and we knew already what we were supposed to discuss. So we did not ask for any details. We did not need any details; we were prepared for the meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So would I be fair to say it wasn't a special meeting; it was just a typical and regular meeting that was set up, I know not by you and the commission. It was set up and you were going to Kiseljak in order to meet with your counterparts to have discussions about POWs and diseased individuals, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: That's how things should have been, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Give me an idea, sir, how far it is from Bijeljina or where your headquarters were for the commission to Kiseljak where this meeting was supposed to take place? What is the distance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: About 200 kilometres to Sarajevo and maybe some 10 kilometres from Sarajevo to Kiseljak, but I can't be sure of that because I'm not that familiar with the plan of Sarajevo. This was the territory under the control of the Croatian Defence Council, and it was populated by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: An approximation will be fine, sir. Thank you for that. Did you ultimately end up going to Kiseljak for this scheduled regular meeting with your counterparts in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: We knew where we were supposed to wait for the UNHCR's APC. We waited, and I believe seven APCs turned up. We did not need as many. I was a bit phased to see so many of them when we only needed two, and then we arrived at the Kobiljaca crossing close to Kiseljak, and that's where we were kept by the military police of the Croatian Defence Council. They asked for our IDs, we told them that we were members of the Serbian Exchange Commission and then they asked from our escorts, from the UNHCR to open the flaps because we were closed inside so that we wouldn't see the lines of our opponents. We waited there for some two hours, nobody turned up, nobody told us anything and finally they told us that the Tuzla commission had not turned up, that the state Muslim commission had not turned up, the representatives of the UNHCR had crossed over to the other side. They wanted us to cross over, one of the officers asked us to wait. We didn't know what we should do until the moment when communication with the Main Staff was established and then we learned that Srebrenica had fallen, that we should not pose any problems and that the two APCs should be let through. They went in the direction of Kiseljak. We were not in a very enviable position. We continued towards Mount Jahorina, and on the following day, we had a meeting at Sarajevo airport. The other side had claimed that they had attended, that they had turned up for the meeting. And we did not reach any agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, we were going to get to the 12th and -- right when we finish the 11th, that's the next topic I hope to cover. Let's just focus for a little bit on the 11th of July, when you were there with the UNHCR. Did they always provide escort to you and the members that came to undertake these negotiations? Did they always provide that escort?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Only on those couple of occasions when we went to the airport, that's when they arrived with APCs to take us through the combat lines to the airport. As for other talks or negotiations, there was no need for them to escort us. It was up to us to make sure that everything was calm and peaceful when we went for these negotiations. They only took us to Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you spend the night that night in Kiseljak or in an area near Sarajevo, meaning the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Somehow we returned to Ilidza and we didn't know what to do. We were supposed to pass through the territory which was part of the Federation, then we had to pass by the trenches of their army although the troops were not there. And we decided to go, we drove at a high speed and that's how we avoided any fire. No fire was open on us because they probably did not know who it was and then we crossed over to the area where we took some forest roads and maybe after 150 or 160 kilometres later, after having driven for that distance through forest -- on forest roads we arrived at Mount Jahorina where we were supposed to spend the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And it may be just my curiosity but why didn't you just go back home, why did you spend the night somewhere, was there any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: We cancelled our accommodation at Jahorina and we planned once everything is done to go back to the places we had come, because the families and parents awaited us there to learn whether we had agreed on anything. However, we were told that we were supposed to go to Jahorina and spend the night there so that the next day we would meet again with the other side on the Sarajevo airport. It was a problem for us because we had to go all the way back because of the vehicles -- because our vehicle from Banja Luka which we had used remained there. We did not plan for another meeting the next day but following the request of the state commission president and because the need was such, we adhered to it, trying to deal with some things at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many people were in this group with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: From Banja Luka, from the 1st Krajina Corps, there were two. Then myself, that's three. Three. But there were some from the state commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You can just tell me if you remember, or if you don't we'll move on, if you remember just give me, was there five, more than five? You can approximate, we'll accept that from you. It was a long time ago. Was it more than ten. We don't need to you list out exactly where they were all from unless it's necessary but first give us an idea of how many people were there, more or less than five?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Maybe seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, you had this meeting scheduled, not you, you didn't schedule it we got that, but a meeting was set up -- yes, I know. And the meeting was set up and the other side didn't show up on the 11th of July, 1995. And they told you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And they told you the reason was because Srebrenica had just fallen; correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: We weren't told that that was the reason for them not showing up but before even returning we did learn of that event. However, it wasn't related to the reason of them not showing up. We were just told they did not show up and that we were supposed to go back, no further explanation was given. The next day they told us that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the next day, sir, meaning the 12th of July, 1995, did you go back with the group and have a meeting with your counterparts to discuss POWs and bodies? A yes or no may even help.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: There was a meeting at the airport. Two presidents discussed the general problems concerning Sarajevo. There was no possibility to go into more specific things. There was also a wish to go on with the negotiations, but pending the Srebrenica event, questions that were to be raised, we subsequently had several meetings with them without the mediation of the state commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let's just stick with this meeting for the moment. Where was this meeting at, you said at the airport, which airport?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I know it may seem obvious sir, but I just want to make sure that I don't lead you and I get that information from you. How long did that meeting last?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In the building of the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Right. And how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. Perhaps an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your counterparts from Tuzla or the Federation, were they present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: From the Federation there were people from the state commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many, if you could estimate to the best of your recollection, and just the number for now, how many people from your counterparts from the Federation were present at this meeting on the 12th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I think there were some from the state Federation commission, there were five. Based on what had been agreed upon in Kiseljak, the people from the Zenica canton were supposed to be there but they did not arrive. I think there was one representative from Tuzla. I only know that nothing was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But share with us -- although there was not an ultimate agreement reached as a result of those negotiations, share with us, if you will, some of the discussions that were being conducted, if any, during that meeting or during those negotiations? What was discussed, if anything?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: We discussed the exchange problems in general. Specifically, we were supposed to talk about the bodies of killed soldiers, that was always a burning issue which still remains unresolved until the present day partly. Some representatives of the state commissions had their agendas, but the event I mentioned prevented them from dealing with the items. The only thing that was agreed was that we were to continue negotiating after a while but we did not set a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then what happened after the meeting concluded, sir, what did you and your group or that group that you were a part of, what happened? Did you leave or stay, or ...

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Once the meeting was closed, we went to our destinations. I went to Bijeljina together with the president of the commission from the 1st Krajina Corps who went onwards Banja Luka. It was on the 12th. We went as far as Vlasenica, and then we were told that we could not go on because there was fighting in the area. There were obstacles on the road preventing us from passing; however, did I talk to them and persuaded them to let us through. I was able to reach Milici there was a joint checkpoint there manned by the police and the military police, and then we couldn't go any further. Among other things, one could hear infantry weapons being fired and mortar shells. My parents -- the parents waited for me for two days. I told them I had to go and ask who could make a decision on me passing through, they told me the military brigade commander. I asked to see him and I explained him that the parents were waiting for me for two days. He allowed us to pass, of course at our own risk. We, indeed, set out and we were rather lucky, we drove fast and were not hit. But there was -- there were some bullets fired over our heads. We reached our destination and I was able to tell the parents what the situation was and what we were expecting to happen. It was that evening. The next day I went to the corps in the morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, sir, in a second. If you don't mind, I just want to ask you a couple more questions about your return to Bijeljina on the 12th. And you mentioned the parents, that you were meeting with parents, and I think I know what you are trying to say but I'm going to have you explain it as opposed to me summarizing it for you. Did you have routine and regular meetings with this group that you identified as "the parents" in your position as president of the Commission for Exchange and Bodies?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I will try to briefly explain. I did have such meetings but they were not planned. For example, in Ugljevik municipality there were 66 that had been taken prisoners and they formed a committee, that was the committee of the parents of those captured and including some politicians there. They were very interested in the exchanges as opposed to Bijeljina which was not particularly interested in the exchanges of soldiers. After three or four meetings with them, I would go to Bjivec [phoen] and the parents and family members would attend. I would explain to them how far ahead the negotiations were. For example, Tuzla offered to exchange five and then I would tell them if you want five to be exchanged, you should decide who the five would be. And then they would refuse, and then the number would increase to 15. They rejected that as well. I didn't want to state who was to be exchanged because then they would ask me why this one, not that other one; it would make things more difficult for me. But we managed to pull through at great satisfaction for the parents. We managed to get those kids back in total. In the area of Bijeljina, the parents organised themselves, as well, and the door was always open. I would only go to the corps occasionally and go back. There was always someone there, either myself or the secretary to provide information. If I left to negotiate, there was at least someone there, and there was always a group of people waiting the results, and I would always explain to them, although I often returned very tired. It functioned well, in particular with the Ugljevik municipality. Of course, I did ask them not to protest or cause trouble. Occasionally people were protesting, demonstrating because no exchanges were taking place, but usually it was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Mitrovic, for that answer. You -- that was part of your basic job duties, if I can say that, to meet and to assist the parents if they had any issues or concerns, which they obviously had given your answer there, from time to time. On the 12th when you arrived to Bijeljina in your headquarters, did you immediately meet with these parents and give them an update as to any questions they may have had regarding their loved ones that were being held in the Federation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: When negotiating, irrespective of what the time of day was because sometimes negotiations were taking place 200 kilometres away, but always I went to the commission first, and even though occasionally it was rather late, there were always groups waiting to hear what the outcome was. In particular on this occasion, we couldn't get by any information. The secretary was waiting there, and they awaited my return. They were explained what the situation was. What was important for them was to know what the situation was and that we would do our utmost. We were at war, and we were facing the opposing party, but we only saw this as a humanitarian issue. We discarded any politics, and I believe it was only good that we did not allow any politics to meddle with what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, I want to show you an exhibit, and it's -- I know we are still talking about July of 1995, but I want to clarify a couple of issues in 1993 when you first became a member of this commission and ultimately its president, so if I may request that 2D520 be brought up to the screen. Sir, you just give me an indication of when you get that document, and tell me if you are able to see it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe we do have a draft English translation. I have a draft English translation, and I thought that we were going to make available to pass out if we didn't have it on e-court for everyone. And if the Court will just bear with me, I'll try to find it. Or it may be just as fast if I just place it on the ELMO, the one that I have, although I have to say that I did make a slight mark on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that would be better. In fact, you could have heard probably Judge Prost precisely suggesting that. Let's do that. It's quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Mitrovic, as she is putting this on the ELMO, that's English translation, and thank you for focusing on the computer screen in front of you, which is the e-court B/C/S version. Just to get an idea about this document, it obviously mentions as you see there the camp at Batkovic. Do you see it at the top third paragraph on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Collection camp, but the name was Collection Centre of Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll call it that, sir; and can you just tell me whether you can identify, and if we can just maybe scroll the document down, from who -- who wrote this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Chief Major-General Manojlo Milovanovic. He ordered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the sum and substance of what -- to the best of your knowledge sitting here, what he was ordering there to the East Bosnian Corps and to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
