utterances.text: It was normal that the chief or commander orders their subordinate, who was the commander of the corps. They were not issuing orders directly to the commission. This was standard procedure. We know in that situation who was responsible for what, who issued the order, who implemented it. This was quite a regular thing for an armed force in which things worked properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just leading up to, actually, the next exhibit, Mr. Mitrovic, which is 2D521, and it's a document that we also have an English draft translation. With the Court's permission, we'd like to use the usher to place on the ELMO, as well, and that's dated the -- we'll take a look. The draft translation has a date on it, but I would like us to just look at the B/C/S version because I think the date may be somewhat inconsistent. And, Mr. Mitrovic, when you get the chance, you tell us when you've had the opportunity to look at this document, and then I'll ask you some questions about it. If you could scroll down, please, ELMO as well. Thank you, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with it. I wasn't the president then. This was a communication between the commander and the president. I do know this document, though. Given that these corps brought their prisoners to us, the predecessor of mine who was the president of the commission used those prisoners in exchanges, as well, not taking into any particular consideration what the needs of those corps were. However, this exchange took place, and the Drina Corps, for example, objected. They wanted that their captured be exchanged, but we were not in a position to do that. However, we were supposed to respect that, to take it into account. And in the subsequent period, it was no longer possible to take prisoners from another area, to have them exchanged without an approval, and there was some part to be played by the corps in that approval, the corps from which the prisoners had come from, from their areas of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions to follow up on your last answer. You said there's some part played by the corps, but given that last paragraph wouldn't it be the corps' call, that they had to be included and involved in more detail, in greater detail than just playing a small part?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This reflected the reality as it was. People from Batkovic, POWs from Batkovic were exchanged who had been captured by the second corps, and the 2nd Corps wanted exchanges, but frequently they would go to somewhere else to be exchanged. Therefore, the corps that had provided the prisoners was not able to have anyone exchanged subsequently. This was only to introduce some order when it comes to exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so we have the date of the document, sir, in English I think the date was typed incorrectly on the day, but I think it's October 1993. But if you would be kind enough to help us and read what the date is on the top of the document 2D521 that we are referencing. You see it on the top left-hand corner, fourth line from the top?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I think the 8th of November. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Or the 8th of October, 1993, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll take a better look at it if we could zoom in on it, but I think it's anywhere from we thought initially 16th or the 23rd of October, 1993. But I don't know that it matters by that many days. But the thing that I'm trying to focus on is that the year is 1993, and that is the time that the Drina Corps, at least to your knowledge being a member of the commission, initially objected as to how they can or cannot bring captured POWs to the Batkovic camp or detention centre.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I think the previous order was implemented. It could have been the Banja Luka or some other corps, but in any case, if they had prisoners and some of their soldiers who had been captured, they asked not to be forced to go as far as Batkovic if they were in a position to establish contact with the other side and to quickly exchange those people in a matter of a few days. Then according to what I know ... I don't think it was done poorly, but if it was at all, the same procedure, regular procedure was followed. There was a request sent from the corps to the Main Staff and the state commission, and once it was approved it was done, of course. The difference may have been in a matter of a few people who were to be exchanged at a later date, and the rest were brought to the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, any time between now and another four minutes when it's convenient for you, we'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm just going to try to get through a little bit more here, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back now to the 12th of July, 1995. During that time period, did you ever come to learn or were you ever informed as to whether or not there were going to be POWs brought into the Batkovic camp or detention centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just ask the question, sir. It might go a little faster. Thank you for your patience in that regard. By whom were you advised of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The chief of security of the corps. I met him, and he told me of the fact that an order was received and that the preparations were carried out in Batkovici to have 1.300 captured Muslim soldiers accommodated in two hangars in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your recollection, can you tell us -- this happened, obviously, after the 11th and after the 12th when you returned back to Bijeljina, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if it happened on the 13th in the morning, afternoon, or evening?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's been 13 years since. I can't tell you what the time was, but after my return -- it wasn't on the 12th, that's certain, but I don't know at what time on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During the day sometime on the 13th. We'll accept that, sire. Thank you. Do you know -- can you tell us who it is that you had this conversation with and from which corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: From the East Bosnian Corps, the chief of security. He conveyed it to me. He knew what problems I had concerning the exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Just -- I need to just get the name before we break for a little period to take a rest. Can you just tell me the name of the individual?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Milenko Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it might be a good time to take a break now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a -- we need 30 minute break, which will start from now. That is, now it's ten to 12.00. We'll reconvene 30 minutes from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, how much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My idea is to try and finish with this witness today if it is possible. I don't know if there are other cross-examinations, but otherwise, we'd have to keep him here waiting until Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we're hoping not to do that, Mr. President, but me and my learned friend did have a discussion about that, and we might -- or we do need the COURT'S guidance on that because I don't know how long the Prosecution has, and I certainly want to give him the opportunity that he needs. I've tried to move it along as best as I can, so perhaps if my learned friend from the Prosecutor's Office can address that issue without me speaking for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, I was going to ask the Prosecution as well, yes. What is your forecast?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. The forecast is gloomy, unfortunately. We had been in discussions about the possibility of myself interviewing the witness in advance of his testimony. We had considered doing that today as we were operating under the schedule that seemed to be pretty reasonable in terms of the examination schedule. We are both obviously taken by surprise by the movement of events, so I've not had an opportunity to interview the witness. That's water under the bridge. However, I was given the lest of exhibits finally late, late last night and was only able to get them together this morning and review them during the witness's testimony. Based on what I've seen so far, I'm going to be at least an hour, I would say, on cross if not more, and where I think we're just getting into what seems to me to be the relevant portions of the testimony. We're frankly being taken by surprise by some of the testimony that goes way beyond the 65 ter summary, so my representations to you are obviously qualified because I don't know what this witness is going to say. And I fear that my estimates will go up and not down, so unfortunately, I think consistent with the conversations I had with my friend earlier this week, we are going to have to keep this witness here, which is what we had planned in any event over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the same time, I would suggest to you in particular to do exactly what I had suggested to Mr. Nikolic earlier on in the day, to distinguish the wheat from the chaff, see what's relevant to this case and forget the rest because we will allow ourselves to be concentrating on what is relevant and certainly not intend to waste time on what is not. So let's proceed, and we'll take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we are going to try our best to finish today. Just be, as you have been, patient with the question. Just give me a short, if you don't mind, answer, and of course, if you need to elaborate and explain, the Court will most certainly give you that opportunity. Now, we left off that you got a message or information from Milenko Todorovic that there should be preparations made for I think you said 1.300 POWs that were going to be placed in Batkovici. Can you tell me, sir, to the best of your recollection what if anything did you do after you received that information from Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I received information and was looking forward to that. I was not duty-bound to do anything. It was the camp command that was supposed to do things. This was just information for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know and were you familiar with whether or not the camp command made any preparations to the Batkovici camp in connection with this new information that was received that there were going to be 1.300 or so POWs brought to the detention centre, Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that. The second hangar had been prepared, cleaned, and prepared to receive them because it was estimated that not everybody could fit in the first hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and let me just quickly show you P117 on e-court, and as that's being pulled up I just give quickly what the document is so we can save some time. It's dated the 13th of July, 1995, and it's an order that seems to be signed by Milenko Zivanovic. And sir, I'm going to just focus your attention quickly once we have it up on the second full paragraph right before it states that "There is an order." It says the paragraph preceding that, it starts "During the night of 12 and 13, July 1995." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you look at this document, sir, although you didn't author it, it's -- you are saying you got this information on the 13th. In fact, you couldn't have got the information before the 13th that there were going to be POWs because the Drina Corps itself only learned late July 12th and early -- late July 12th and July 13th, 1995, this there were going to be forces that they may capture; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, now, just looking at the first paragraph of the order, could you just help us with that. In that first paragraph, I'd like to focus everyone's attention on the seconds line of that order. It's discussing the fact that the brigade commands in their area of responsibility will employ all available able-bodied men to do the following, sir: "... discover, block, disarm, and capture any Muslim groups observed and prevent their crossing into Muslim territory." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was, sir, consistent with what Mr. Milenko Todorovic told you on the 13th of July, 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's just go back quickly to the preparations, if any, that were made in the Batkovic camp, and I know you didn't make them, sir. That was the commander's responsibility at that detention centre. Can you tell me, in addition to just adding or bringing or opening another hangar, what if anything to your knowledge was done at the Batkovici camp in preparation for these 1.300 POWs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the accommodation was prepared in the second hangar. The material supplies had already been provided for the corps reserve. Food was prepared, and it was expected from the ICRC to help with the clothing and all the other preparations in respect of the hospital conditions. Everything had been planned should the need arise in the course of the event. In any case, there were capacities and provisions to accommodate that many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And ultimately, sir, were POWs brought to the Batkovici camp from the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was already the second half of the month after the 15th or the 18th when the first group of 20 was brought in, mostly wounded. They had already been taken care of in the area where they were captured, I suppose, so when they arrived in Bijeljina they once had already been dressed and any additional aid had been administered, if necessary. I believe it was on the 20th when they arrived. I did not go to the corps, but I was told that there were 20 POWs, and I said that I couldn't do anything with the 20 because I had 101 in Tuzla. And after a certain while, not to take up any more of your time, later on we received a total of 167 prisoners, so we could offer them for exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And they were all from the Srebrenica enclave or thereabouts, correct, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me show you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The 167.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Let me show you an exhibit, 3D17. And as we are getting that exhibit up on the screen, sir, I think there's -- and I'll just briefly identify it. It seems to be a list, and it has certain information on it, so I would ask that it perhaps not be a public broadcast because I'm not sure of the sensitivity of the names. So just with that caution, but we'll look into that, and I think it's already been accepted in evidence. Sir, in this list of POWs that were brought to Batkovici, or so it seems, there's a certain date that says "odlazak" or "dolazak," which is when they arrived at Batkovic, and "odlazak" when they were released or left Batkovic. If you could just help me, if we look at the first few pages, and I'll give you the exact page number. There are indications that POWs were brought to the Batkovic detention centre as early as the 18th of July, 1995, and maybe if I give an ERN number, that would help, and that would be this Document 3D17, ERN number 0357-2256. And I'm merely highlighting this, I think, throughout the document, Mr. Mitrovic. We do see the entry dates of when they were admitted into the Batkovic camp, but I'm looking at that one because it seems to have a group of maybe five or so, six individuals that were brought into Batkovic that day. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In July, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: There were more of them who were brought on that day. I believe that some 20 of them. I can't be sure, but I know that that's when the first group arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, I'm just showing you a portion of the list, sir, and if you'd like and if --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Okay, then. Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the Court permits, I could hand you the list, but it's just -- on the screen we can only take it one page at a time. So what I'd like to know, sir, and if we could go back to the first or second page of this document, again, ERN 0357-2252, which is the first page of when the list starts identifying individuals and places thereof they're from and information such as when they arrived at the detention centre. This list, sir, help me with this. Is this the list to the best of your -- did you ever see this list before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't see the list. If this arrived in Batkovic, it was part of the normal procedure. The corps or whoever sent POWs would send a list and an accompanying document. In other words, I did not have to see this list if I wasn't in Batkovic, but I knew how many there were. And later on, I went there to take the particulars of all of them, which was what the Tuzla commission requested from me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And, sir, on this list as you can see, and just help me understand, it shows the place where these individuals, these POWs were from, right? It identifies Srebrenica, Zvornik, Bratunac, and other areas throughout the list. Am I reading that correct? That's all I just want to know from you at this point.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It should be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you remember when was the first time that ICRC was given access to the POWs at the Batkovic camp in July 1995 or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date. There were no bans on visits, and I believe that it was after the arrival of the last groups once the situation had been consolidated. I believe that it was around the 25th or the 26th; in any case, when after the last groups arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And I think you are actually -- memory serves you better than I had thought. 2D, if we can have, 522.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we're just briefly to show this document, Your Honour. This is a document in English, and it's from the ICRC which identifies this date. I just wasn't certain the witness was able to recall that it was approximately the 25th or 26th when ICRC had access. I believe this document assists us in that regard. So... and if we can just have the second page of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir -- and actually the third paragraph. I apologize. I thought there was a carryover. It says in this document, sir, it's in English, and I'm not sure if you can read English, but I'll it read for others here as well. It's in this -- third paragraph of page 2, it says "ICRC has granted access to prisoners from Srebrenica ..." And on the third line below that, it says that "These negotiations in order to obtain access finally bore fruit on 26." Do you see that? No? Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This document, sir, is obviously dated, for the record, the 27th of July. I might have the wrong first page on it, but we'll check that. Sir, my question to you is, what happened to the 160 or so POWs that were in Batkovici after the fall of Srebrenica when they were turned over to that detention centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: They were received in the collection centre, and I was in contact with the Tuzla commission. I don't know the date, and they asked for all of them from Batkovic to be handed over. I believe there were some 220 or 30 of them for the 101. I couldn't accept that. I reminded them that through all this time in negotiations, pointed out the request of exchanging one fighter for one fighter. In the meantime, a group of 45 was transferred to Kotorsko, to the area of the 1st Krajina Corps, because they had an immediate need for an exchange. However, things may have been -- there were two or three delays. There were several meetings, and finally it was agreed for the 27th of September, delayed for the -- rescheduled for the 29th of September. And on that occasion we received 66 men, and we gave them the 20 wounded plus some 20 people from Srebrenica, and we also gave them those who had been there from before from other areas, from Cazin, Kladusa, and other places. So for their 66 we gave them our 88, which was only normal because what we received were indeed fighters, and what we gave them were people who might have participated in initial fighting. So it was a fair exchange that had been agreed upon on both sides. As for the rest of the people in Batkovici, they would be subject of negotiations between the Krajina corps and the commissions of the Tuzla and Zenica compound. And we finally managed to agree to fit in everybody from Batkovic where I had 35 of those who were supposed to be returned to me, and there was a need on the part of the 1st Krajina Corps for the rest of the detainees. At the end of the day, there was an exchange in which we managed to exchange everybody from Batkovic and the people from Zenica in the Kotor prison in Doboj; and also on the 24th of December, 1995, Batkovic was closed down because the last group had been exchanged in Sockovoc near Gracanica. That's where the exchange took place between the Tuzla commission, the commission of the Zenica council, and the 1st Krajina Corps, and our commission, and that was the end of the story of Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and thank you for sharing that with us. I just want to go back on two points, and clarify this for me: You mentioned the 29th of September, 1995. That's when the POWs that were captured, the Bosnian Muslim military men that were in Batkovic, that's when they were ultimately exchanged to their counter -- or to their -- to be brought back home. Is that correct? They were exchanged to either Tuzla or somewhere in the Federation, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That was the last date. I know there were other exchanges before that. I just want to get that as timeline. And then also, sir, I think you told us that the Batkovic camp ceased to exist and was closed as of the 24th of December, 1995? Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- I think as you told us in your testimony earlier today that you continued to work in this position as President of the commission until I think you said 1997. Is that correct also?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, during the time from 1995 when Batkovic detention centre was closed and up until the time you remained in 1997, were you dealing with, obviously, deceased POW -- deceased soldiers and individuals in an exchange with the your counterpart in Sarajevo or Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, I misspoke. Tuzla. And your counterparts continued to negotiate and meet with you similarly to that which you've testified here already earlier, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I thank my learned friend for allowing me to ask those questions. Let's me ask you something about the Geneva Convention, sir, and I'm not asking you to give me your legal opinion. Do you remember at that time at all having discussions with Milenko Todorovic or others at the East Bosnia Corps? Was there ever a discussion about Geneva Conventions and complying with that when dealing with POWs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No, this was not discussed. However, already 1993, the first or the second time I went to Batkovic, I had an occasion to see that brochures had been left there by the ICRC. I read them, and I know that everybody read them. There were brochures, and this existed in our army even in peacetime. They were informed about that, both the soldiers and the officers, and it was the officers' duty to convey to the foot soldiers the message on how to treat prisoners of war. This was already present during peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just show you, if I may, P107. Let's see if I can -- let's see if this document is familiar to you or not, and it's dated the 2nd of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with the Court's assistance, if we can go directly to page 7 of the document, although the document is ten or so pages long. I think just for our purposes we would focus on that at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm showing you a document from, again, Milenko Zivanovic who was the Drina Corps commander at that time dated the 2nd of July. AND there's many things in this document, but for our focus I'd like just to read out this sentence on the 7th page that's in English and in B/C/S. It says "In dealing with prisoners of war and the civilian population, behave in every way in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that a typical -- given your experience in dealing with the corps and your experience in the military and that which you've shared with us relating to your background, is that a typical-type order that would be given by a corps commander for active combat activities, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I am not an active serviceman, but as far as I know this would be the sequence when it came to preparations for combat, although this was issued to the 2nd Corps that I didn't belong to. Maybe it would be best to provide explanations about that, but I would say that this is customary and this was in keeping with the military regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's move, then, away from this document, and let's look at P, 33 and as it's being called up, it's a document dated the 9th of July, 1995. It seems to have been authored by Zdravko Tolimir, although the English version, I believe, misspells his name. And this is, sir, on top as you can see on this document - thank you - it's from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska dated the 9th of July, 1995. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... it's indicated here, at least in the English, very urgently to, among others, the president of the Republika Srpska for information, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is focus with you, given the period of time that we have left, the last sentence in the last paragraph of this document. And just so the record is clear, Mr. Mitrovic, this is obviously being sent, also, to the Drina Corps command as you can see.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this had nothing whatsoever to do with the East Bosnia Corps or the commission for exchanges as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we'll get to that in a second, sir. The Main Staff of the army would have from time to time sent, if you know, to the East Bosnia Corps certain information or directives or orders on how they should comply, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in this one, Mr. Tolimir apparently on the 9th of July, 1995, proceeds to tell the Drina Corps the following among other things: "Ban the torching of residential buildings and treat the civilian population and war prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949." Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: That's what I read, and it -- this has been repeated several times, that Geneva Conventions should be abided by.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, sir, and I think you mentioned it, but I just wanted to be clear: Did you ever receive a complaint from ICRC as to whether or not the POWs that were in Batkovici camp were mistreated in any fashion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Never, either from the ICRC or from the commissioner of the Tuzla Canton. I never learned myself from other sources that something of the kind happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am trying to rush through. Thank you for your patience. I just didn't get a good feeling as to -- and I don't know if you may have answered, and forgive me for asking it again. I know you said that at one point there were approximately 800 POWs that were in the Batkovici camp while you were president or a member of this commission. Can you just tell me, during the period of time that you were there, from 1993 through, let's say, 1995, how many Bosnian Muslim POWs were exchanged with your counterpart?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: This was reduced by the time I joined the commission as its president. Only 50 remained in Batkovic. The rest had been exchanged, but that was done during the time while I was still not the commission's president.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the POWs, the number that you gave, were exchanged, those 50, correct? There weren't some that you were holding back. I mean, you exchanged everything that you had, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic, thank you very much for your patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I'll conclude here in the interests of trying to have him go home this week or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You just mentioned, sir, about the ICRC documents. Do you know how it is that they were distributed to members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Am I supposed to answer that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If the question made sense to you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer? It has been pretty much limited now, so I suggest that you try and finish by quarter to 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My name is Nelson Thayer. I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sorry we didn't have a chance to meet. I was hoping to, but that's life, and let me get underway with my questions. If I understood the military service history that you shared with us this morning, you served as head or chief of security, it sounded like, in a couple of brigades, partisan brigades; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In one brigade and in a division. Actually, it was a division that was disbanded, and then I joined the brigade; and before that it was the civilian security or the state security where I was professionally engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, turning your attention to your service on the commission for exchange. Can you just tell us, was that a civilian position, or was that a military position?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It was a military position because we were involved with the exchanges of prisoners of war and not of civilians. It was a military position, but the president of the commission was also appointed by the establishment, and the rest were from other units, the other three that were members of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So when you were serving both as a member and then later as the president, were you, for example, in uniform?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I also attended negotiations in uniform and sporting my rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And that was in July of 1995 -- what, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: All the time. I would never wear civilian clothes when I went to negotiations, always uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question was, and in July of 1995, what was your rank, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, I believe I was either major lieutenant-colonel in -- a reserve lieutenant-colonel, that is, either/or. Both promotions followed each other in a very short sequence. I was either major or lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And so you were -- just to make sure there's no misunderstanding, you were a uniformed member of the East Bosnia Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And to what extent during your service in that capacity did you interact with the security organs at any level, be it from the Main Staff, to the corps, to the brigade, or even below?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The only interaction was with the corps. If there was something of importance for the commission, then it went via the chief of security of the corps directly in communication with the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no contacts with the Main Staff and the security administration directly. It always went through my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you say your superior, to whom are you referring, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: While I was a member of the commission, as I was told I came to the corps to be a member of the commission, but the establishment post I was assigned to was a desk officer for security of the corps. As I've said, there were people from other units in the commission, and this was on top of their regular duties, and the same applied to me until the moment I became president of the commission. I went between the corps and the office that was downtown. That's the office where we would receive citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, I'm not sure this came out entirely clearly, but when you referred to the office, where was that office located, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The office was in Filipa Visnjica Street. I don't know what number of the -- what the number of the house was. 14, I think, four or five houses down the street from the office where the ICRC premises were. I would pass by their office to get to my office. That was a cafe/bar that they occupied. It used to be a cafe/bar which had a door to the street so that everyone who wanted to could get by the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what city was this in? What city are we talking about, sir, or town?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: All right. And to whom would you report in the corps? Who was your immediate superior in the corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Milenko Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, we've obviously heard testimony about this collection centre or camp or prison. I want to show you a photograph. This is 65 ter number 3521, and while we are waiting for that to get uploaded onto e-court, sir, can you describe for the Trial Chamber, please, approximately where is this camp located, just -- geographically so we can orient ourselves.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: From Bijeljina, some 10 kilometres northeast to the Sava. You go by Batkovic, the settlement of Batkovic, and you come across the area that was the cooperative of Batkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, do you see an image before you on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you see an image before you on the computer, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And is that to your recollection an aerial image of the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It seems to be, sir, yes. The buildings closest to us are the two small warehouses, and then the following four out of those, two had already been full of grain, wheat. They were in regular use because crops had to be placed somewhere, and in one of the remaining two we had the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We are done with that exhibit. And if we may have 65 ter 3522, please. Sir, do you see a document in front of you that is --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- dated 13 March 2002?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you were shown previously a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have a translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We do. It's being uploaded but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- I can work with the ELMO if we need to, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could do that if it's going to take time to upload it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, frankly, I don't think I will be really referring to many pages so I won't need the ELMO for a moment. I think we can work with the B/C/S. Sorry, Madam Usher, actually I will need your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to hand you a hard copy in your own language of this document. You were shown another list of prisoners from the Batkovici prison camp, that was 3D17. I want to show you another document. And if you could just turn the cover page over, and if, sir, I could direct your attention to the very first page of this list.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you see the heading where it says: "List of Muslims exchanged from the Batkovici collection centre." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the column, and it's the second column in from the right, it says: "Date of departure from the Batkovici collection centre." I've highlighted just that heading for you. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm being informed that the English is available now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it under seal? Your list cites it as under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, this is under seal, Judge Kwon. Thank you for the intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Kwon. So there will be no broadcast of any of the pages from this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And before I start asking you a couple of questions about this document, sir, looking at that column under date of departure from the Batkovici collection centre, we see some dates that are repeated over and over again. Can you see that, sir? We have some prisoners being exchanged on the 12th. There's another group, it looks like, on the 12th of September, sorry. Another group on the 24th of December, and we see another group that appears to have been exchanged on 7 October. Do you see those general groups, sir, those common dates of exchange?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to point out what I think may be a typo on the very first line under the name "Alada Alic," [phoen] it indicates that he arrived in Batkovic on the 18th of July, and I believe that's consistent with what you testified earlier that there were a number of prisoners that began arriving after the 18th or on the 18th. Then it indicates that he departed from the camp on 10 July. I would just suggest to you and see if you agree that that is just a transposition of the date and day and that is it should actually be October 7th, like the other people that were exchanged on October 7th? Certainly he couldn't have arrived on July 18th and been left on the 10th. Would you agree with that, just to get that typo out of the way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you recall receiving any explanation from the East Bosnia Corps security chief, Mr. Todorovic -- and forgive me, I forget his rank, was he a lieutenant-colonel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving any information or explanation as to why it was not until July 18th or afterwards that prisoners from Srebrenica began arriving in the Batkovici prison camp?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't told why and as a subordinate I had no right to ask and I didn't. I didn't ask what the reason of their late arrival was. It was up to me to say, "Yes, sir." That is where things stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to share with you some excerpts from statements provided by two prisoners who wound up in the Batkovici camp, and if you could just look at your hard copy there, sir, and I'll give you their names and you can identify them with me. If we go to entry number 113?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, do you see the entry for Sead Hasanovic, son of Huso?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: From Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And he arrives, according to this record, on or about the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I also want to turn your attention to the entry at number 124, if you can locate that, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Very well, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you see the entry for Ramo Osmanovic, son of Ramiz?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it indicates that he was brought to the camp on the 26th of July. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just -- and if I may have the -- Madam Usher's assistance. Do we have the English on e-court. Does everybody have that? Okay, then. Thank you. I won't need your help. If we go just to the first page of -- if we can have 3519, please. We see here -- and do you have it in your own language, sir, the first -- the front page there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: A witness statement by a Ramo Osmanovic, son of Ramiz?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... the year 1976?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 5 of this statement, and it will be the last paragraph in the B/C/S, in the actual statement portion, just before the witness acknowledgement. And that's actually page 5 in both the English and the B/C/S, so it will be just before that witness acknowledgement that we are seeing there. My apologies sir. We are getting you the proper page on e-court right now. Should be the -- just the page before the -- page 5 of both B/C/S and English. And about midway through that big paragraph, sir, it refers to being surrounded by Serb soldiers at around 0830 hours. Do you see that, that section, sir, where it refers to that time? I'm just calling that out to you as a way of orienting you in the paragraph, if you see the time 0830, and if you --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And -- Mr. Osmanovic told the investigators that when they got to a temporary holding place or prison in Osmaci, it says that "In the prison we had found the four comrades that had been captured previously. One of the prisoners asked the policeman what would happen to us, and he answered that we were very lucky because the order that had been given by General Mladic was that all the prisoners captured by 18 July had to be executed, and those captured after the 18th had to be arrested and detained." You see that there, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we may go to 65 ter 3518, and I'll ask you a couple of questions about that document and then finish up on this topic, sir. We see here a statement by Sead Hasonovic, and if we turn to the second page, do you see, sir, at the top of the page in your own language where it refers to -- he says, I am Sead Hasonovic, son of Huso. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Born in 1964. If we could --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 4 of the English, please, and that's also 4 of the B/C/S. And there's a reference to a Sapka, a type of military hat or head dress. Do you see that word, sir? I'm just trying to orient you. It's a very long, dense paragraph.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You've located it, sir? Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see where it says, "The leader of the patrol said to me, 'You are very lucky that you were captured by this corps,' and that they had been issued instructions from the authorities the previous day that they had to stop killing those prisoners who were captured as well as those captured previously and not yet killed. The instruction was issued to keep the captives alive to use us for prisoner exchange." Do you see that there, sir?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, just to orient you to the date that he is referring to or the approximate date, if we could go back to page 3, and this will be in paragraph 6 of the B/C/S, and you've got it there. Towards the bottom, there's a reference to about 400 people gathered. He refers to it being about the fifth or sixth day after setting out from Susnjari, and I would submit to you that it's the Prosecution's evidence that this would place the date of this witness's capture on or about the 18th of July, 18th or 19th of July. Now, sir, my question to you is, having heard these excerpts from these two prisoners, two separate prisoners captured in two different locations, both of whom wound up in Batkovic, saying essentially the same thing about prisoners being ordered not to be executed after a certain date, does that ring any bells with you? Does that refresh your recollection at all about any information you may have heard about why it was that prisoners didn't begin arriving at that camp until on or about the 18th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I don't know of such an order ever being issued. I doubt that any of the most senior officials would do such a thing. As for the rest of what was happening to them, it was not in the area of the East Bosnian Corps. I as the president of the commission was not in a position to know what was happening in another territory. I am sorry for what happened to those people. It's a tragedy, but it's a very wide area, and it was not a topic of my interest. I wasn't supposed to be interested in such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Well how about the 13.00 prisoners that my friend asked you about that you told us about you had been expecting? You testified that General Tolimir had indicated to your security chief to expect these 1.300 prisoners, but what we've heard about so far today was, I think, somewhere around 200 Srebrenica prisoners that may have been exchanged at some point. What happened to the other 1.100 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: They didn't arrive. It was an estimate. That many had been estimated to arrive in Batkovici, but I don't know what actually happened. The others also did not arrive when we expected them, and I was looking forward to their arrival because of the exchanges that were pending. Only 20 arrived later on in the evening, and they were all wounded. Later on, there was some pressures to bear from the president of the neighbouring municipality. They were willing to go to the area to capture and to use them for exchange. The corps commander refused that, and he said that he would send a unit of the military police and that their task would be to capture and not to kill, to capture at all costs, making sure that none of ours got killed. However things may have been, we received that number and we could perform the exchange, and I was glad that the 1.300 arrived. We would have handed them over without any exchange, actually, because there was no reason for them to be kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe I'm a little confused, but you started out at line 1 of page 74 saying that the 1.300 didn't arrive, and if I understand what I'm reading, you are saying now that they did arrive at some point? Where did they arrive, sir? Or maybe it's just a translation or transcription error, or maybe it's just Friday.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: It must be a translation problem. Nobody arrived before the 18th, although we expected them. Everything had already been prepared for the 1.300, and then on the 18th only 20 wounded came. And it was only after the 18th, on the 23rd, 24th, that the others came, and that was it. That was all. There was no more. I don't want to go into great length. There are some other dates here. I believe that a group of 45 were handed over to the 1st Krajina Corps and they were taken to the prison in Kotorsko so that they could exchange them for those people in Tuzla. And finally, they were joined with the rest of ours, and that was the exchange on the 24th of 12 when the last prisoner left Batkovici and when Batkovici was closed down as the collection centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sir, you're, I take it, familiar with the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You're familiar, sir, with the general geography of this area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, are you not, the area from Bijeljina down to Zvornik? Driven that road many times, I presume?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Not many times. Every time I went to the sea, I went via Tuzla, and the rest of the area that later on belonged to the Federation. I did take that road several times before the war, and I know the area to a certain extent. I don't know any of the hamlets or villages. I'm familiar with the bigger settlements like Zvornik, but I'm familiar with the road from Zvornik to Milici, Vlasenici, and that area. That's where I went through.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you estimate for the Trial Chamber, please, about how long would it take to you drive from, say, Zvornik to the camp at Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: The distance is about 60 kilometres. I can't give you an estimate. It all depends on the speed and on the type of vehicle, on the quality of the driver. In any case, the distance is 60 kilometres of an asphalt road. That would be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you just told us that those 1.300 prisoners never arrived as you had expected. I want to show you one last document and ask you some questions about it along those lines, and that is P00175. This was a document that was on my friend's list of documents, so I don't know if you've been shown it or not, but I'm going to show it to you. Do you see the document in your own language in front of you, sir? It's a little --

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we can just scroll down a little bit on the B/C/S -- I mean, sorry. Scroll the other way, thanks, so we can just read the top. Sir, we can see that this is a report to the Drina Corps command dated 12 July 1995, and this is from the command of the Milici Brigade. If you could, sir, just take a moment to read through this document, please. It shouldn't take too long. It's pretty much just that first page that you see there in your own language.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: This also doesn't refer either to my area or to me as the president of the commission. This is the area of the Drina Corps so that -- I don't know what I could tell you about this. This was not sent to the East Bosnia Corps but to the Drina Corps. If I had been the president of the state commission, then the story would be different because that person had jurisdiction over everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why don't you wait for the question, please. Your question, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, this document is dated 12th of July. I believe you've already testified about what you were doing that day and when you received this information that you say you got through General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: you, does it not, that he is in the custody and control of the Milici Brigade of the Drina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I may be mistaken, but I don't remember that the witness ever said that he had received such information from General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I believe I said it was through General -- or from General Tolimir but obviously through his chief of security. I don't think we need to quibble about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, both. Let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, this individual who is described as a prisoner of war on the 12th of July within the Drina Corps, you would have expected him to be one of these 1.300 soldiers or civilian prisoners that you had been told to expect, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again, we can see that his name is (redacted) (redacted). May we have P03517A, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This needs to be in private session or just not broadcast, Mr. President, whichever is easier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's easier either way, so let's not broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Bear with us, sir, while it's coming up on e-court. I can tell you, you are definitely going home today.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't asked Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's 3517A. I'm sorry. I thought I called out for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't asked Mr. Ostojic if he has got a redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see a document in front of you? It's just a couple of lines, and I'll help you with it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: 1 January 1977. Date of disappearance, 11 July 1995, in the forest. Sir, this document is Prosecution evidence of the remains of this individual being recovered and identified through DNA evidence, recovered from a mass grave in the area of Cancari. Prosecution's evidence is that this individual was a victim of a mass execution. Did you receive any information during this time that mass executions were being committed in the Drina Corps zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: No. One could assume that bad things were happening, but I did not receive information to that effect from anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, why could one assume that bad things were happening? What information did you have, or what led you to assume that bad things were happening during this time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I'm starting from the fact that we were expecting 1.300 to arrive in Batkovic and they failed to arrive. We didn't know why they didn't arrive, and we could only assume that something happened to them if there was an estimate of that number. And if you will allow me, I would like to say something else. If something was indeed happening, it was not very wise to make any inquiries, especially on my part. I was a reserve officer. I was not that interested in the politics, and if the civilian bodies had learned of me expressing any sort of interest, I would not have fared that well. So I had to refrain myself from asking any questions. I was never very much in favour of walking around Bijeljina and making inquiries. That's why I never maintained contact with Tuzla. I tasked with my deputy to do that. I always avoided such tricky situations that would have cost me something.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So, sir, you've got security experience, and you served on this commission, had a lot of experience with prisoner exchanges. Do you know of any reason to divert thousands of prisoners of war from Batkovic instead of back to Batkovic and housing them in little schools around the Zvornik area? Do you have any explanation why that would have been done, thousands of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBOMIR MITROVIC
utterances.text: I have no explanation, and if we are talking about executions, I don't believe that anybody from the command had ordered that. And as for the evil that took place, I'm very sorry that this happened. I'm sorry for all the people that fared badly during the war, but there were individuals who acted of their own will, who did not respect any command, who did not obey any orders. They just did as they pleased, and I believe that as a result of that some bad things happened. The behaviour of such individuals caused some of those bad things to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thayer. Mr. Ostojic, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, in the interest of seeing this witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- get home this weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. Ostojic, and behalf of everyone I wish to express our gratitude that you all cooperated to make it possible for this gentleman to return home to his family. On behalf of everyone Mr. Mitrovic, I would like to thank you for having come over, and I also wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you very much for your understanding, and thank you for allowing me to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we do the documents next time? All right. Okay. Exhibits, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would ask that Exhibit 2D520 and 2D521 and 2D522 be introduced into evidence. The other exhibits that I've used I believe are already introduced into evidence, so I'm only calling for those three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. They are so admitted. They are all translated, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, they are in draft -- two of them are in draft translation. One is in English. I just want to check the date on the ICRC it said -- has a different date that I think is just an error on their part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Any documents on your part, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We do, Mr. President. We have 65 ter 3517, which is under seal; an excerpt that we showed today, 3517A, and that is also under seal; we have 65 ter 3521, that is the aerial imagery of the camp; 3522, that is the list of Batkovic prisoners shown to the witness; 3519, one of the witness statements shown to the witness; 3518, another witness statement shown to the witness; and P00175, the Milici report, Milici Brigade report that was shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Ostojic, or any --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think -- if this is about the statements...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. Certainly the portions that were quoted and the front page that was shown to the witness are the only portions we need placed in evidence, just to establish if there's any question. But we don't need the whole statement in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I still object to the statement or any portion of it going in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if questions were put and answered...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I realise that they were put to the witness, if they were put to the witness for things other than what they are going to ultimately try to use because they obviously see a -- in my opinion, a hole in some -- in their claim that they were orders being distributed, and what they're trying do is to bring in evidence through these witnesses in connection with that. I do object to that. Those witnesses, if they could come and testify on that very critical issue, but for using it for that purpose I think is highly prejudicial and, quite candidly, improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wouldn't put it quite like that with respect to my learned friend. What I would submit is, first of all, the relevant passages have been read out, read out very slowly by my learned friend, and therefore, they are in evidence. And secondly, if the Court was against me on that, then the Court has previously admitted certain documents on a very limited basis vis-a-vis the impeachment of a particular witness, but I hope I can win on my first point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think -- is it on the same matter, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Simply to say that I fully agree with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I think the fact that the relevant parts were read out and answered doesn't require the introduction of the documents in the record. In other words, what we have in the transcript itself should suffice. All right. The others, any objection with regard to the other documents? We hear none, so they are all admitted provided they are all translated, which I think they are. Thanks. We stand adjourned until Wednesday. In the meantime, Mr. Ostojic, you've been approached by our senior legal officer on some things we would like you to attend to. You have got a short break to do that. Otherwise, we will have to clamp down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I've answered the question to him, and I think all those witnesses will and should belong on our 65 per list, but I'll look specifically at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 1.52 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of July, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.
